L27: # Current Clinical Trials
L28: 
L29: The Blue Buffalo Veterinary Clinical Trials Office (BBVCTO) supports studies that help advance the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of diseases in animals. Clinical trials at The Ohio State University Veterinary Medical Center are funded by a variety of sponsors, including university researchers, foundations, and industry partners. Opportunities for participation change throughout the year and may be available for pets with a variety of health conditions.
L30: Clinical trials managed by BBVCTO are independent of the Blue Buffalo company and do not imply the use or evaluation of Blue Buffalo products unless specifically stated in an individual study.
L31: 
L32: Interested in participating? Browse our currently enrolling studies or complete the Pre-Screening Questionnaire to determine whether your pet may qualify for an active clinical trial.

L8: # Oncology Clinical Trials
L9: ## What are clinical trials?
L10: 
L11: Clinical trials are a type of research.  They are an important component of all specialties of medicine and help us as researchers and veterinarians to evaluate new types of diagnostics and treatments.  Clinical trials are variable and may be designed to answer different questions including is a new treatment more effective, is a new diagnostic more specific, or does a new therapy combination have less side effects.
L12: ## Who can join clinical trials?
L13: The Lois Bates Acheson Veterinary Teaching Hospital has many clinical trials underway at any one time.  It is possible that a pet may be eligible for more than one ongoing clinical trial.  There are often initial tests such as a physical exam, blood work and/or imaging that are needed to ensure a patient is approved for enrollment in a trial.  All clinical trials have a unique set of inclusion and exclusion criteria that help the research team enroll the correct patient population.  Your pet’s oncology clinicians will discuss standard treatment and clinical trial treatment options with you.  It is your decision as to whether or not you would like your pet to participate in a clinical trial.
L14: ## What are the benefits of participating in a clinical trial?
L15: 
L16: There are several important benefits to participating in clinical trials.  You and your pet will be personally involved in expanding the scientific knowledge of oncology in veterinary patients.  Your pet may also receive novel diagnostics and/or treatments, and may receive these services at reduced or no cost.  The potential benefits of a clinical trial are varied and would be discussed thoroughly prior to your pet’s enrollment.
L17: ## Contact information:
L18: 
L19: Please do not hesitate to contact the teaching hospital and the oncology service for more information on clinical trials.  If your pet has been diagnosed with cancer, we are available to discuss clinical trial options with your referring veterinarian in more detail.
L20:

L25: ## Current Trials
L26: 
L27: ### Pilot Study Evaluating the Microbiota in Dogs with Lymphoma
L28: #### Study Purpose:
L29:   * The gut microbiome is essential in maintaining the health and immunity of the host.  Alterations in this population of microorganisms and in mucosal tolerance have been shown to be a potential driver in the pathogenesis of many infectious and inflammatory diseases as well as certain types of cancer.
L30: Specifically related to cancer, the human and canine gut microbiota has an active role in drug pharmacokinetics, cancer therapies, and related toxicities.  Limited data exists in the veterinary literature related to the microbiome in dogs diagnosed with lymphoma.
L31:   * The goal of this study is to evaluate differences in the microbiota between healthy dogs, dogs with lymphoma, and dogs with lymphoma treated with chemotherapy. Additionally, the impact of chemotherapy on the microbiota and eventual relapse will be examined. Evaluation of this information will determine whether changes in the microbiota after treatment is a significant prognostic factor for adverse effects from chemotherapy, response to therapy and response duration.
L32: #### Inclusion Criteria:
L33: 
L34:   * Dogs diagnosed with naïve multicentric lymphoma
L35:   * Dogs at least 1 year of age and minimum weight of 15 kilograms
L36:   * Dogs must be otherwise healthy, and have adequate bone marrow and organ function
L37:   * Owners must sign consent form
L38: 
L39: #### Exclusion Criteria:
L40: 
L41:   * Dogs that previously received chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy for lymphoma treatment
L42:   * Concurrent malignancy or other serious systemic disorder incompatible with this study
L43: #### Study Protocol:
L44:   * Dogs will need a physical exam, complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and confirmation of lymphoma and immunophenotype to ensure eligibility for enrollment.
L45:   * Dogs must be treated with either the 19- week CHOP or single agent doxorubicin chemotherapy protocol
L46:   * Once enrolled, dogs will have nasal, oral and rectal swabs performed throughout the study protocol.
L47:   * Once the chemotherapy protocol is completed, the dog will be rechecked with a physical exam, nasal, oral and rectal swabs as well as tumor response monitoring monthly until relapse is documented.
L48: #### Financial Incentives:
L49: 
L50:   * Clients with enrolled dogs will have special financial considerations.
L51:   * Patients, once enrolled in the trial, will have discounted examination fees.  Clients are responsible for all other costs associated with their pet’s treatment including enrollment tests and examination, other recommended blood work, chemotherapy, treatment of adverse events and ancillary medications.  Detailed estimates of cost are available upon request.

L172: Osteosarcoma (bone cancer) in dogs is the most common type of bone tumor. Unfortunately, they are highly aggressive tumors, characterized by local destruction of healthy bone around the tumor and spread to other organs such as the lungs.
L173: The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether a new type of radiation therapy combined with an immunotherapy drug called Gilvetmab can safely treat lung lesion(s) (spread from the primary bone cancer) while causing fewer side effects than standard radiation therapy or chemotherapy.
L174: If your dog participates in the study, he or she will receive one dose of FLASH-RT proton radiation to a lung lesion under general anesthesia and 3 doses of immunotherapy (Gilvetmab) given directly into the vein as an infusion. We will obtain different types of samples (blood and lung washes) and diagnostic images (Computed Tomography (CT) and chest x-ray) before and after treatment during the follow-up visits.
L175: 
L176: Inclusion criteria
L177:   * Dogs with confirmed appendicular (limb) osteosarcoma with lung metastases (spread to the lungs) > 1cm that are visible on chest xray after standard of care amputation
L178:   * At least one mass in the lungs must be visible on chest xray > 1cm but the maximum diameter of the largest lesion should be <5cm
L179:   * Dog is free of clinically significant abnormalities on blood work
L180:   * Dog is free of significant other diseases
L181:   * Dog is an appropriate candidate for general anesthesia
L182:   * Dog has never received Gilvetmab before
L183:   * Dog has not received systemic chemotherapy or immunotherapy in the past 3 weeks
L184:   * Dog is on <0.5 mg/kg/day of prednisolone before enrollment
L185:   * Dog does not have bone metastasis
L186:   * Owner is able to abide by all study visits up to 1 year after enrollment conducted at Ryan Veterinary Hospital in Philadelphia, PA
L187: The study will cover the following until the last follow-up visit at 48 weeks post-RT:
L188: 
L189:   *  Study-related exams, imaging, and laboratory tests
L190:   * FLASH-RT (radiation therapy)
L191:   * Immunotherapy (Gilvetmab x 3)
L192:   * Management of complications directly related to the study (up to $500)
L193:   * Autopsy – post mortem examination
L194: 
L195: Owners are responsible for initial diagnostic tests to confirm eligibility such as:
L196:   * Routine bloodwork (CBC and Chemistry panels)
L197:   * Urinalysis
L198:   * Chest x-rays
L199:   * Physical examination
L200: 
L201: The limb with the primary bone cancer needs to be amputated prior to enrollment, and the cost is not covered by the study.
L202: 
L203: Please contact the VCIC for more information at 215-573-0302 or email vcic@vet.upenn.edu .
